```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

```{r setup}
library(winpipe)
```

A named pipe (also called a FIFO for first-in, first-out) is a mechanism for inter-process communication (IPC) that lets two unrelated processes exchange data as if it were a file. Unlike a regular file, however, it does not store data on disk. Whatever one process writes, the other reads in order (first in, first out). 

While the concept of a named pipe exists both on Linux and Windows, named pipes on Windows have some important caveats that make cross-platform R support for them traditionally weak. Windows named pipes:

* are not part of the Windows file system but are reserved a special namespace (`\\.\pipe\*`).
* can be bidirectional, so both sides can read and write.
* have an explicit server/client API with support for multiple pipe instances.
* support access control through security descriptors.
* work over the network.
* support message streams.

Except for network access and message streams (which I think are mostly useless for R applications), `{winpipe}` supports all of these features. For a comparison to existing named pipe implementations, see `vignette("compare", package = "winpipe")`.

# Server and client

You can create a named pipe with the function `winpipe()`. As mentioned earlier, named pipes on Windows can be both server and client. Importantly, only a server can create a pipe while a client can only connect to one.

```{r client-error, error=TRUE}
np_exists("example-pipe")
cli <- winpipe("example-pipe", server = FALSE)
```

```{r server}
srv <- winpipe("example-pipe", server = TRUE)
cli <- winpipe("example-pipe", server = FALSE)
```

A `winpipe` is a standard R connection, which means that reading and writing works out of the box.

```{r connection}
srv
```

```{r read-write}
writeLines("send me a dataset", cli)
readLines(srv)
```

This also means that all wrappers around base I/O work out of the box.

```{r}
write.table(cars, srv)
head(read.table(cli))
```

Similar to I/O, connecting to a named pipe also follows a FIFO principle. Since a named pipe allows multiple instances, one named pipe can be served by multiple servers and listened to by multiple clients. Right now, there is one server and one client. If we tried to connect another client, it would fail because there is no free server available.

```{r client-none-available, error=TRUE}
cli2 <- winpipe("example-pipe")
```

Instead, we need to create another server first, which is able to serve another client.

```{r second-instance}
srv2 <- winpipe("example-pipe", server = TRUE)
cli2 <- winpipe("example-pipe")
```

By doing this, we have created a second instance of the same pipe. You can check the number of instances by inspecting the state of a pipe.

```{r state}
np_state(srv)
```

If a server disconnects, the client loses its ability to communicate through a pipe. The ability of a client to communicate to a named pipe depends on the availability of a server.

```{r disconnect, error=TRUE}
np_connected(cli2)
close(srv2)
np_connected(cli2)
writeLines("hello?", cli2)
```

```{r cleanup1}
close(cli2)
```

# Server privileges

Servers have some privileges when it comes to handling clients. First, they are allowed to _impersonate_ as a client.  By impersonating, they can retrieve information from the clients end. In `{winpipe}`, this is supported through `np_token_info()`.

```{r tokeninfo}
np_token_info(srv)
```

The output contains information about the client's name, SID, group membership, and permissions. The field `impersonation_level` shows us, to what degree the server can impersonate. In this case, client and server are the same user so only identification is allowed.

Second, the server is allowed to disconnect a client without closing the connection. This leaves the server in a disconnected state where it is not able to accept new clients. The server needs to explicitly decide when to listen again using `np_listen()`.

```{r kick, error=TRUE}
# Disconnect client
np_connected(srv)
np_disconnect(srv)
np_connected(cli)
close(cli)

# Client cannot connect again immediately
cli <- winpipe("example-pipe", server = FALSE)

# Only if the server decides to listen again can a client connect
np_listen(srv, blocking = FALSE)
cli <- winpipe("example-pipe", server = FALSE)
```

```{r cleanup2}
close(srv)
try(close(cli))
```

# Blocking

winpipe connections can be set up to wait for requests or responses. Similar to base connections, `winpipe()` supports a `blocking` argument. If set to `TRUE`, the connection blocks the R session until the other side of the pipe responds. To exemplify, I am going to set up a background R session using `callr`.

```{r block-server}
start_server <- function() {
  callr::r_bg(function() {
    message("Waiting for client...")
    srv <- winpipe::winpipe(
      "winpipe-block",
      open = "w",
      server = TRUE,
      blocking = TRUE
    )
    message("A client connected!")
    Sys.sleep(3)
    writeLines("hello", srv)
    close(srv)
  })
}
```

Until a client connects, the server will keep waiting and blocking.

```{r block-waiting}
srv <- start_server()
while (!np_exists("winpipe-block")) Sys.sleep(0.1)
cat(srv$read_error())
```

When a non-blocking client connects, it will return immediately and return nothing because the server did not have the time to respond.

```{r block-nonblocking}
cli <- winpipe(
  "winpipe-block",
  open = "r",
  server = FALSE,
  blocking = FALSE
)

system.time(x <- readLines(cli))

x

close(cli)
srv$kill()
```

When a blocking client connects, it will wait until the server has responded and thus return the server's greeting.

```{r block-blocking}
srv <- start_server()
while (!np_exists("winpipe-block")) Sys.sleep(0.1)

cli <- winpipe(
  "winpipe-block",
  open = "r",
  server = FALSE,
  blocking = TRUE
)

system.time(x <- readLines(cli, n = 1))

x

close(cli)
srv$kill()
```

## Controlling the blocking status

By default, the session is blocked for 60 seconds (`getOption("timeout")`), but you can control the timeout using the `timeout` argument.

```{r block-timeout, error=TRUE}
srv <- winpipe("winpipe-block", server = TRUE, blocking = TRUE, timeout = 1)
```

The timeout can be controlled after pipe creation.

```{r}
srv <- winpipe("winpipe-block", server = TRUE, timeout = 1)
np_set_timeout(srv, 3)
np_get_timeout(srv)

close(srv)
```

Another way to stop blocking, of course, is to interrupt the execution.

```{r block-interrupt}
srv <- start_server()
while (!np_exists("winpipe-block")) Sys.sleep(0.1)
srv$interrupt()
Sys.sleep(0.5)
cat(srv$read_error())
```

A non-blocking winpipe can be made blocking by using `np_listen()`:

```{r make-blocking, error=TRUE}
srv <- winpipe("winpipe-noblock", server = TRUE)
np_listen(srv, timeout = 1)

close(srv)
```

## Peeking

Even when non-blocking the request/response behavior can be controlled using peeking. Peeking allows us to retrieve the size of a payload before reading it and to check _if_ a message was delivered and _how big_ it is. After reading it, the payload is consumed.

```{r peek}
srv <- winpipe("example-peek", server = TRUE)
cli <- winpipe("example-peek", server = FALSE)

writeLines("here is a payload", cli)
np_peek(srv)

readLines(srv)
np_peek(srv)
```

This opens two mechanisms. First, this lets you implement custom blocking reads with callbacks. In this example, the server waits until a minimum payload size of 50 bytes was sent. This allows the client to stagger the request.

```{r peek-minimum}
while (np_peek(srv) < 50) {
  writeLines("and another one", cli)
  message("payload not big enough")
  Sys.sleep(0.5)
}
readLines(srv)
```

Second, it opens possibilities to handle payloads based on their size. In this example, the server accepts only payloads with less than 20 bytes. If the client sends a larger one, it declines and closes the pipe instance.

```{r peek-maximum}
writeLines("here is a really really really big payload")
if (np_peek(srv) > 20) {
  writeLines("payload is too big", srv)
  close(srv)
}

readLines(cli)

close(cli)
```


# Security descriptors

Who may connect to a pipe, and what they may do once connected, is controlled by a security descriptor (SD) that the server sets when it creates the pipe. By default, `winpipe()` uses `sd_default()`, the default DACL of the current token. You can inspect the SD of any pipe with `np_sd()`.

```{r sd-default}
srv <- winpipe("example-sd", server = TRUE)
np_sd(srv)
```

Each entry in parentheses is an access control entry (ACE) that allows or denies a set of rights to an account. To build your own, create ACEs with `ace()` and collect them with `sd_create()`. Accounts can be well-known names such as `"everyone"` or `"local system"`, or a SID. To refer to ourselves, we can read our own SID from the token information, which is available once a client has sent data.

```{r sd-sid}
cli <- winpipe("example-sd", server = FALSE)
writeLines("hello", cli)
readLines(srv)
me <- np_token_info(srv)$sid
close(cli)
close(srv)
```

## Limiting what a client may do

A client opens a pipe with the rights it needs: reading needs read access and writing needs write access. If the SD only grants read access, a client can read but not write.

```{r sd-read-only, error=TRUE}
read_only <- sd_create(ace(rights = "generic read", account = me))
read_only

srv <- winpipe("example-sd", sddl = read_only)

# Reading is allowed
cli <- winpipe("example-sd", open = "r", server = FALSE)
close(cli)

# Writing is not
cli <- winpipe("example-sd", open = "w", server = FALSE)
close(srv)
```

## Locking clients out

ACEs are evaluated in order, and a matching _deny_ ACE overrides a later allow. Here, everyone is allowed access, but we deny ourselves first. As a result, even the user who created the pipe cannot connect to it.

```{r sd-deny, error=TRUE}
deny_me <- sd_create(
  ace("deny", rights = "generic all", account = me),
  ace("allow", rights = "generic all", account = "everyone")
)
deny_me

srv <- winpipe("example-sd", sddl = deny_me)
cli <- winpipe("example-sd", server = FALSE)
close(srv)
```

The same mechanism lets you restrict a pipe to a specific user or group on a shared machine. For instance, to grant access only to members of the local Administrators group, you would use `ace(rights = "generic all", account = "admins")`.
